meta.regime: The regime is no longer simply rising US real rates beating everything - it is rising US real rates beating everything EXCEPT the yen, and the distinction is now the central trade on this board. Friday proved it: the hottest core CPI print in three months pushed CME FedWatch from 69% to 87% for Wednesday's hike and lifted the 2-year to its highest since July 2024, and USD/JPY still closed 0.52% lower. The second feature is that two of the three classic risk-transmission channels have broken. The franc did not bid on a tanker strike in Hormuz, and the Canadian dollar did not rally on a 9% weekly gain in Brent. When the haven currency ignores the war and the petro-currency ignores the oil, what is left is a pure rate-differential market, and the only differential that is genuinely repricing rather than merely being confirmed is Japan's. The third feature is calendar concentration: the Fed, the Bank of England and the Bank of Japan all decide inside 61 hours this week, which means the entire symbol list is effectively one position on how those three land relative to what is already priced.

dailyRead: Two things happened between Thursday's file and this one, and only one of them changed a score - but the one that did not change a score is the more important. US August CPI printed Friday at 12:30Z: headline 3.4% y/y and +0.4% m/m, both exactly in line, but core rose +0.3% on the month against 0.2% expected, a tenth hot and the fastest in three months. CME FedWatch jumped from 69% before the print to 87% for September 16, the 2-year Treasury yield topped 4.6% for the first time since July 2024, the 10-year closed at 4.97% and TD Securities extended its forecast to three hikes in the cycle with the next two in October and January. That is the most hawkish single day the dollar has had this month. DXY closed at 99.122, up 0.07%. And USD/JPY FELL 0.52% to 153.615, finishing the week down 1.69% and the month down 3.65%. The yen won the head-to-head on the dollar's best data day, and that is the cleanest possible evidence for why JPY stays at +3 and USD stays at +2 rather than the reverse. The mechanism is straightforward once stated: the Fed's hike is the third in a sequence and 87% priced, while the BoJ's Friday move from 1.00% to 1.25% takes the policy rate to its highest since September 1995 and opens a path that 62% of surveyed economists now see reaching 1.75% by end-Q2 2027. One is a confirmation, the other is a regime change, and markets pay for regime changes. There is also a real caveat inside the CPI that argues against chasing the dollar: core CPI on the ANNUAL rate SLOWED to 2.4%, the lowest reading since March 2021, down from 2.5%. Energy inflation is 16.3% y/y with gasoline +27.4% and fuel oil +52%, while shelter eased to 3.0% from 3.2% and food to 2.7% from 3.0%. Strip the war out of the index and American core inflation is at a five-year low. That is precisely the split a committee can go either way on, and it is why Wednesday's dot plot rather than Wednesday's hike is the event. The score that DID change is the Swiss franc, cut from +1 to ZERO. The case is a week of evidence, not a single session. A vessel was struck in the Strait of Hormuz late Saturday near Qeshm Island, killing one person and injuring four, with a second vessel hit by an unidentified projectile and UKMTO confirming a fire and crew evacuation. A senior Iranian official dismissed the prospect of fresh talks with Washington. Brent rose 9% on the week. Through all of that USD/CHF rose 0.83% on the week and 0.45% on Friday alone, making the franc the worst-performing G10 currency against the dollar over five sessions. It lost ground to the euro, to sterling, to the Australian dollar and, by 2.52%, to the yen. This file has flagged the franc's failure to bid twice; a third week of it with a tanker burning in the strait is a verdict, not a wobble. The SNB is at 0% with a September 24 hold carrying both TE consensus and forecast, Swiss inflation is 0.8%, and the only live policy lever is the greater-readiness-to-intervene language from June - which cuts against the franc, not for it. CHF goes to 0 and every long-franc expression is closed: USD/CHF is raised to a HIGH-conviction LONG, EUR/CHF, CAD/CHF and AUD/CHF go long, and CHF/JPY becomes a HIGH-conviction short at the intersection of the board's weakest haven and its strongest currency. The second non-obvious break is in Canada. Brent gained 9% on the week and settled around 104 dollars, WTI is at 100.050 with a monthly gain of 20.15%, and USD/CAD still ROSE 0.25% on the week and 0.28% on Friday to 1.38724. The petro-currency transmission has stopped working, and the reason is that a 4.6% US 2-year overwhelms a terms-of-trade tailwind when the Bank of Canada is frozen at 2.25% and just lost 41,700 jobs in a month. The practical consequence matters for position construction: USOIL LONG and CAD LONG are no longer the same trade and should no longer be sized as though they correlate. USD/CAD is therefore a LOW-MED long rather than the short the oil chart would imply, and Monday's Canadian CPI at 12:30Z - consensus 3.0% y/y with the monthly rate expected to collapse from +0.5% to 0.0% and trimmed-mean at 1.9% - is the test of whether the Bank has any reason at all to move. Everything else holds. The euro stays +1: the ECB delivered its second hike of the war to a 2.50% deposit rate, revised 2027 inflation up to 2.5% and 2028 to 2.1%, upgraded growth, and Lagarde said inflation risks are tilted to the upside - and EUR/USD still closed the week at 1.15985, down 0.14%. A central bank that hikes and revises up while its currency drifts lower is a currency that is already fully paid for its hawkishness, which is why the euro is a fine funding leg against the kiwi and the franc and a poor one against the dollar. Sterling stays at 0 after Friday's upgrade, and this week will test it hard: Tuesday's labour report at 06:00Z is expected to show unemployment RISING to 5.0% from 4.9% with average earnings including bonus FALLING to 3.9% from 4.1%, while Wednesday's CPI at 06:00Z is expected to show inflation RISING to 3.1% from 2.9% with core at 2.7%. Rising prices into a loosening labour market is the textbook definition of a frozen central bank, and TE carries a 0/9 vote-cut and 3/9 vote-hike consensus for Thursday's Bank of England decision at 11:00Z. Sterling is neutral because both of its tails are live, not because nothing is happening. Australia holds at +1 on its own stated trigger: copper deteriorated further to 6.4695 with the monthly return now -1.93% against -1.42% on Thursday, but the second half of Thursday's condition - a soft domestic employment print - has not been met and cannot be until mid-October, so the score does not move on one leg. AUD/USD at 0.71676 is still +7.42% year-to-date. The kiwi stays the board's only negative and was the worst major of the week at -1.16%, which is the more interesting result because New Zealand carries the HIGHEST headline inflation in the G10 at 4.1% and just hiked to 2.75% on September 2. The market is simply refusing to pay for it, and the domestic data explains why: unemployment rose to 5.6%, consumer confidence collapsed to 80.4 from 94.7, retail sales fell 0.5%, the manufacturing PMI slid to 53.1 from 54.3 and building permits fell again. The RBNZ itself said core inflation, wages and expectations remain consistent with a return to the 1-3% band by mid-2027 and TE carries a HOLD for October 28 with the next move not until December 9. A central bank hiking into a consumer recession does not get a currency bid, and NZD/JPY at -1 against +3 remains the widest and cleanest gap on the board.

USD.when: Sept 16, 18:00Z - TE carries consensus AND its own forecast at 4.00%, and CME FedWatch is 87% after Friday's CPI, up from 69% before the print and 60.6% on Thursday
USD.note: TE re-verified this morning: policy rate 3.75% upper bound, CPI 3.4% y/y with +0.4% m/m and core 2.4% y/y, unemployment 4.1%, non-farm payrolls +162,000, GDP 1.5% q/q and 2.1% annual, manufacturing PMI 53.9, services 56.5, retail sales -0.6% m/m, consumer confidence 47.8. USD HOLDS AT +2 rather than being raised, and the reason is a result rather than a forecast: this was the dollar's best data day of the month and it still lost the head-to-head to the yen, with USD/JPY closing -0.52% and the week -1.69%. The hike is no longer the question - at 87% it is priced, and TE's own forecast agrees. The question is the Summary of Economic Projections, because TE's projection rows still carry 3.6% for the first year and 3.4% for the second against 3.8% current, which is a dot plot that implies EASING after this hike. Warsh has refused forward guidance since Jackson Hole on August 28, where he said the predominant focus should be on prices and that he was concerned underlying inflation trends had not improved, so the dots are the only guidance the market will get and they carry unusual weight. There is a genuine dovish hook inside Friday's print: core CPI on the annual rate SLOWED to 2.4%, the lowest since March 2021, with shelter down to 3.0% and food to 2.7%, while energy inflation ran at 16.3% - a committee that wants to look through an oil shock has the data to do it. TD Securities went the other way and now forecasts three hikes with the next two in October and January. Both readings are defensible from the same print, which is exactly why conviction is capped at +2.

EUR.when: Late October - the ECB hiked on September 10 and the next monetary policy decision follows the September 30 non-policy meeting and the October 8 accounts, with nothing on TE's calendar before then

That is a hawkish package by any reading, and EUR/USD closed the week at 1.15985, DOWN 0.14%. The euro is fully paid for its own central bank. Thursday's final August HICP at 09:00Z should confirm 3.3% with core at 2.4%. Lagarde speaks Monday at 15:15Z, Wednesday at 17:00Z and Friday at 10:30Z, with Schnabel, Cipollone, Buch, Vujcic, Elderson and Lane also on the tape - an unusually heavy speaker week in which any softening of the further-tightening language is the euro's main downside risk.

geopolitics: The war entered the weekend with a fresh escalation and one live de-escalation track running simultaneously, which is why oil is elevated but no longer trending. Late Saturday a commercial vessel was struck near Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, killing one person and injuring four according to Iranian state broadcaster IRIB, and the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations Centre confirmed that a second vessel was hit by an unidentified projectile, with a fire breaking out aboard and local authorities helping evacuate the crew. A senior Iranian official dismissed the prospect of fresh negotiations with Washington, and President Pezeshkian repeated that the strait will reopen only if the United States ends its naval blockade; President Trump has said the state of the waterway is acceptable for now with the US Navy escorting tankers. Shipping through the strait has been largely blocked since February 28, and Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority still claims no vessel may pass without a permit it issues. Against that, officials from Iran and Gulf states meet in Muscat on MONDAY to sign an agreement establishing an Iran-Oman shipping route through the strait - a partial, bilateral workaround rather than a settlement, but the first scheduled de-escalation event in weeks and the reason crude sold off into the weekend. The price action tells the story precisely: Brent gained 9% across the week to settle around 104.610 and WTI reached 100.050 with a monthly gain of 20.15%, and then both fell hard on Friday, WTI -2.37% and Brent -2.81%, as the Muscat meeting was confirmed. Urals is at 103.70, up 8.31% in a session. The FX transmission is where this week's most useful finding sits, because two of the three channels have stopped working. The Canadian dollar did NOT rally on a 9% weekly gain in Brent - USD/CAD rose 0.25% to 1.38724 - because a US 2-year above 4.6% overwhelms a terms-of-trade tailwind when the Bank of Canada is frozen at 2.25% and shed 41,700 jobs in August. And the Swiss franc did NOT bid on a burning tanker: USD/CHF rose 0.83% on the week, the worst G10 result against the dollar, which is the evidence behind today's CHF downgrade to zero. What still works is the inflation channel. US energy inflation is running at 16.3% y/y with gasoline +27.4% and fuel oil +52%, and that alone is holding headline CPI at 3.4% while core annual falls to 2.4%, the lowest since March 2021 - the war, not the US economy, is what is keeping the Fed hawkish. The same mechanism drove the ECB's second wartime hike and the RBNZ's, and the RBNZ explicitly called its 4.1% inflation fuel-driven and temporary. European gas remains the secondary channel: EU gas at 79.52 euros per MWh is +30.32% on the month, German gas at 80.65 is +29.32% and UK gas at 198.26 pence is +32.25%, though all three fell about 3% on Friday - enough easing to lift the DAX 0.82% and upgrade GER40 from SHORT to RANGE, not enough to change the direction. Practical read: keep USOIL long but at MEDIUM rather than HIGH conviction into the Muscat signing, stop treating CAD as an oil proxy, and do not hold the franc for war protection it has now declined to provide three weeks running.
